# Why this note exists {.unnumbered}

The definition of a measure assumes that a countably additive set function is
already available on a sigma-field. In practice, measures are usually first
specified on simple sets:

- lengths of intervals;
- probabilities of half-open intervals determined by a CDF;
- products of probabilities on rectangles;
- masses assigned to finitely many categories.

The **measure-extension problem** is to turn those simple assignments into a
genuine measure on the full sigma-field needed for probability and
integration.

This is general foundation material for a statistician. It is **not required
to decode Walker's notation**. Walker uses measures that have already been
constructed. Read this note when you want to understand where Lebesgue
measure, product measures, and probability laws come from.

## What this note assumes

Read [Measure and probability foundations](measure-probability-foundations.qmd)
first. The companion note
[Generating sigma-fields and the pi-lambda method](generating-sigma-fields-and-pi-lambda.qmd)
explains generators and uniqueness arguments. No real-analysis course is
assumed.

# The construction problem {#extension-problem}

Suppose $\mathcal C$ is a simple collection of subsets of $\Omega$ and a set
function $\mu_0$ has been proposed on $\mathcal C$. We want a measure $\mu$ on
$\sigma(\mathcal C)$ such that

$$
\mu(A)=\mu_0(A)
\quad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal C.
$$

Three issues must be separated:

1. **compatibility:** the proposed values must obey the appropriate additivity
   rules;
2. **existence:** at least one measure must extend those values;
3. **uniqueness:** no different measure should have the same starting values.

The definitions below identify the compatibility needed for extension.

# Rings and algebras of sets {#rings-and-algebras}

A nonempty collection $\mathcal R$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is a **ring of
sets** if

1. $A,B\in\mathcal R$ implies $A\cup B\in\mathcal R$;
2. $A,B\in\mathcal R$ implies $A\setminus B\in\mathcal R$.

These rules imply $\emptyset\in\mathcal R$ and closure under finite
intersections. A ring need not contain the whole space $\Omega$.

An **algebra of sets** is a ring that contains $\Omega$. Because

$$
A^c=\Omega\setminus A,
$$

an algebra is closed under complements and finite unions. A sigma-field is an
algebra that is additionally closed under countable unions.

| Set class | Finite unions | Differences | Contains $\Omega$ | Countable unions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Ring | Yes | Yes | Not required | Not required |
| Algebra | Yes | Yes | Yes | Not required |
| Sigma-field | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Finite unions of half-open intervals form a useful ring on $\mathbb R$. They
are easy to measure by adding interval lengths, yet they do not contain every
Borel set.

# Content, premeasure, and measure {#content-premeasure-measure}

Let $\mu_0$ be a nonnegative set function with $\mu_0(\emptyset)=0$.

A **content** is finitely additive on a ring or algebra:

$$
\mu_0(A\cup B)=\mu_0(A)+\mu_0(B)
\quad\text{when }A\cap B=\emptyset.
$$

A **premeasure** is countably additive whenever the disjoint sets and their
union all belong to its ring or algebra. If $A_1,A_2,\ldots$ are pairwise
disjoint and $\bigcup_nA_n$ is still in the domain, then

$$
\mu_0\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_n).
$$

A **measure** is a countably additive set function whose domain is a
sigma-field.

The correct implication, when the domains are aligned, is

$$
\text{measure}\Longrightarrow\text{premeasure}
\Longrightarrow\text{content}.
$$

This is a chain of increasingly strong requirements, not the reversed set
inclusion sometimes suggested by informal diagrams. A measure has both a
larger type of domain and the countable-additivity property.

# Finite additivity is not enough {#finite-not-countable}

Let $\Omega=\mathbb N$ and let $\mathcal A$ contain every finite subset of
$\mathbb N$ and every cofinite subset, meaning a set whose complement is
finite. Define

$$
\mu_0(A)=
\begin{cases}
0, & A\text{ is finite},\\
1, & A\text{ is cofinite}.
\end{cases}
$$

This is a finitely additive probability content on $\mathcal A$. However,
each singleton has mass zero while

$$
\mathbb N=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{n\}.
$$

Countable additivity would require

$$
1=\mu_0(\mathbb N)
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_0(\{n\})=0,
$$

which is impossible. Thus finite additivity alone does not support the limit
operations used throughout probability.

# Continuity of a measure {#measure-continuity}

Countable additivity implies two limit properties.

## Continuity from below {#continuity-from-below}

If

$$
A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq\cdots,
\qquad
A=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n,
$$

then

$$
\mu(A_n)\longrightarrow\mu(A).
$$

To see the mechanism, split $A$ into disjoint increments:

$$
A=A_1\cup(A_2\setminus A_1)\cup(A_3\setminus A_2)\cup\cdots.
$$

Countable additivity turns the partial sums of increment masses into
$\mu(A_n)$.

## Continuity from above {#continuity-from-above}

If

$$
A_1\supseteq A_2\supseteq\cdots,
\qquad
A=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n,
$$

and $\mu(A_1)<\infty$, then

$$
\mu(A_n)\longrightarrow\mu(A).
$$

The finite-mass condition prevents the undefined subtraction
$\infty-\infty$. For a probability measure it holds automatically.

For a finite content on an algebra, continuity at the empty set is a useful
test for countable additivity: if $A_n\downarrow\emptyset$ always implies
$\mu_0(A_n)\downarrow0$, then the content is a premeasure.

# Outer measures {#outer-measures}

An **outer measure** $\mu^*$ assigns a value in $[0,\infty]$ to **every**
subset of $\Omega$ and satisfies

1. $\mu^*(\emptyset)=0$;
2. $A\subseteq B$ implies $\mu^*(A)\leq\mu^*(B)$;
3. for arbitrary $A_1,A_2,\ldots$,

$$
\mu^*\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)
\leq\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu^*(A_n).
$$

An outer measure need not be additive on all subsets. Its purpose is to give
an upper size to every set by covering it with simple measurable pieces.

Given a premeasure $\mu_0$ on a ring $\mathcal R$, define

$$
\mu^*(E)
=\inf\left\{
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_n):
E\subseteq\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n,
\ A_n\in\mathcal R
\right\}.
\tag{1}
$$

The infimum is the smallest achievable upper bound from countable covers. It
plays the same role as taking the best approximation from outside.

# Caratheodory-measurable sets {#caratheodory-measurable-sets}

A subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is **Caratheodory measurable** for $\mu^*$ if
for every $E\subseteq\Omega$,

$$
\mu^*(E)
=\mu^*(E\cap A)+\mu^*(E\setminus A).
\tag{2}
$$

Equation (2) says that cutting any test set $E$ along $A$ causes no loss or
overcounting of outer size.

The Caratheodory-measurable sets form a sigma-field, and the restriction of
$\mu^*$ to that sigma-field is a measure. This is the decisive step: outer
measure is defined everywhere, while genuine additivity is retained on the
subsets that pass criterion (2).

The proof is important in a real-analysis course but is not needed to use the
result in statistics.

# The Caratheodory extension theorem {#caratheodory-extension}

In a commonly used form, the theorem says:

> A premeasure on an algebra extends to a measure on the sigma-field generated
> by that algebra. If the premeasure is sigma-finite, the extension is unique.

A premeasure $\mu_0$ is **sigma-finite** if the space can be covered by
countably many domain sets of finite mass:

$$
\Omega=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n,
\qquad
\mu_0(E_n)<\infty.
$$

Probability premeasures are automatically finite and therefore sigma-finite.
Lebesgue length on $\mathbb R$ is sigma-finite because

$$
\mathbb R=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}[-n,n]
$$

and each interval has finite length.

The theorem separates the jobs cleanly:

- the premeasure records compatible values on simple sets;
- the outer-measure construction supplies existence;
- sigma-finiteness supplies the standard uniqueness guarantee.

# Constructing Lebesgue measure {#constructing-lebesgue-measure}

Start with half-open intervals and assign

$$
\lambda_0((a,b])=b-a.
$$

Extend this assignment additively to finite disjoint unions of such intervals.
The resulting set function is a premeasure on a ring. The outer-measure
construction (1) and Caratheodory criterion (2) produce Lebesgue measure
$\lambda$ on a sigma-field containing all Borel sets.

This explains why the familiar rule “interval length equals endpoint
difference” legitimately extends to very complicated measurable subsets of
the real line.

The resulting Lebesgue sigma-field is larger than the Borel sigma-field
because it also includes every subset of a Borel set of Lebesgue measure zero.
For most statistical calculations, the distinction can remain in the
background.

# Constructing a probability law from a CDF {#constructing-law-from-cdf}

Let $F$ be nondecreasing, right-continuous, and satisfy

$$
\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,
\qquad
\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x)=1.
$$

On half-open intervals, propose

$$
P_0((a,b])=F(b)-F(a).
$$

These values extend to a probability premeasure on an interval algebra and
then to a probability measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. Conversely, that
measure has CDF $F(t)=P\{(-\infty,t]\}$.

The extension theorem supplies existence; the
[pi-lambda argument](generating-sigma-fields-and-pi-lambda.qmd#cdf-determines-law)
supplies an efficient uniqueness proof.

# Why this matters in statistics {#extension-statistical-relevance}

Measure extension sits behind familiar facts:

- a valid CDF determines one probability law;
- probabilities specified on rectangular events determine joint and product
  laws;
- interval length extends to Lebesgue measure and hence continuous densities;
- consistent finite-dimensional laws can sometimes define a stochastic
  process on an infinite product space.

The last item requires an additional extension theorem for stochastic
processes. The pattern is the same: specify compatible probabilities on a
manageable class, then extend to a much larger event space.

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. How does an algebra differ from a sigma-field?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Both contain the whole space and are closed under complements and finite
unions. A sigma-field is additionally closed under **countable** unions. An
algebra is often a manageable starting domain for a premeasure.
:::

**2. Which implication is correct among content, premeasure, and measure?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

On aligned domains,

$$
\text{measure}\Longrightarrow\text{premeasure}
\Longrightarrow\text{content}.
$$

A measure is countably additive on a sigma-field. A premeasure has the needed
countable additivity on its smaller ring or algebra, and every countably
additive set function is finitely additive.
:::

**3. Why does the finite/cofinite example fail countable additivity?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Every singleton has mass zero, but their countable disjoint union is
$\mathbb N$, which has mass one. Countable additivity would incorrectly force
$1=\sum_n0=0$. The example is finitely additive but is not a premeasure.
:::

**4. Why is the finite-mass assumption needed for continuity from above?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The usual proof subtracts the limiting intersection from the first set. If
$\mu(A_1)=\infty$, that can produce the undefined expression
$\infty-\infty$. Probability measures always satisfy the assumption because
$P(A_1)\leq1$.
:::

**5. What is the different role of an outer measure and a measure?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

An outer measure assigns an upper size to every subset and is only guaranteed
to be countably subadditive. Its Caratheodory-measurable sets form a sigma-field
on which the outer measure becomes countably additive and therefore a genuine
measure.
:::

**6. What does sigma-finiteness contribute to the extension theorem?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

It supplies the standard uniqueness guarantee. If the space is a countable
union of finite-measure pieces, two extensions agreeing with the same
premeasure cannot differ on the generated sigma-field. Probability
premeasures are automatically sigma-finite.
:::

**7. In constructing a probability law from a CDF, which steps provide
existence and uniqueness?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The interval increments $F(b)-F(a)$ define a probability premeasure. The
Caratheodory extension theorem extends it to a Borel probability measure,
providing existence. Agreement on the generating half-lines, followed by the
pi-lambda theorem, provides uniqueness.
:::
